title: Demystifying the Resilience of Large Language Model Inference: An End-to-End Perspective
problem: LLM inference resilience to bitwise faults is poorly understood; aggregate metrics mask significant quality degradation in text generation despite model resilience claims.
motivation: Prior resilience studies focus on classification models; commercial-scale LLM inference resilience to random bit-flips requires characterization to enable fault-tolerant deployment.
method: The researchers injected random single-bit errors into the numerical weights that make up a language model, then had it generate text and measured what happened in two ways: standard accuracy metrics and actual text quality degradation. This revealed whether the model was truly resilient or just appeared okay on traditional measures. They tested across different task complexities to see whether harder tasks broke down more easily under bit-level faults.
key_novelty: Language models appear resilient based on standard accuracy measurements, but actually generate degraded and meaningless text when hit by random bit-flips, with the damage severity depending on how complex the task is.
contributions: First comprehensive bit-flip fault study on commercial-scale LLM inference
Demonstrates disconnect between accuracy metrics and actual text quality degradation
Shows complex reasoning tasks (CoT, MoE) suffer more from faults
End-to-end analysis from parameter faults to output quality
limitations: Abstract-only; unclear on fault injection depth, specific models tested, or remediation strategies
